docs.text:
h2

Per-trait liability-scale heritability, diag(G).

docs.title: genetic_cov property
docs.text:
genetic_cov

Additive genetic trait covariance G.

docs.title: env_cov property
docs.text:
env_cov

Within-person residual trait covariance E (excludes C/M).

docs.title: correlations property
docs.text:
correlations

Each component matrix standardised to a correlation (NaN for negligible variance).

docs.title: rg property
docs.text:
rg

Genetic correlation matrix, G standardised.

docs.title: re property
docs.text:
re

Residual environmental correlation matrix, E standardised.

docs.title: rp property
docs.text:
rp

Within-person liability correlation: the sum of all component matrices.

docs.title: fit_pairwise_multi
docs.text:
fit_pairwise_multi(families, *, components=('A',), sampling=None, weights=None, phen_names=None, eps=1e-06, maxiter=300, tol=1e-10)

Fit joint heritabilities and genetic/residual trait correlations.

Each member needs one bound per trait and a common threshold per trait; uninformative traits contribute no pairs. components contains A and optional C/M. Component matrices are PSD with unit total variance and residual eigenvalues at least eps. phen_names labels the traits.

The independent-family and population/IPW contracts match fit_pairwise. maxiter and tol control SLSQP and stationarity checks. Interior fits return family-cluster/delta-method SEs; any covariance boundary withholds them. Composite likelihood does not support ordinary likelihood-ratio tests.

docs.title: Assumptions, checklist & pitfalls
docs.text: What the model does and does not represent, a pre-flight checklist for a production run, and the common mistakes.

docs.title: Modelling assumptions
docs.text:
By default, the high-level predictor uses additive genetic sharing only: every off-diagonal entry is shared_DNA × h² (the optional c2/m2 shared-environment components below add their own off-diagonals). It assumes jointly Gaussian liabilities, correct relationships and diagnoses, and correctly specified prevalence/CIPs and liability-scale h². Under its standard model, individual-specific residuals are independent of relatives' additive genetic values and of each other.

Diagnosis quality and family-history reporting are therefore part of the observation model, not clerical details. An Alzheimer-disease proxy-GWAS analysis documented bias from survival and non-random participation in parental-history surveys (Wu et al. 2024), while a broader psychiatric-genetics Perspective argues that shallow EHR or self-reported phenotypes can carry heritable confounding (Cai et al. 2026). Liability modelling alone cannot correct a biased diagnosis or reporting process.

The age-dependent formulation assumes a non-decreasing cumulative-incidence curve (hence a non-increasing liability threshold) and, in the current high-level model, the same liability covariance and genetic architecture across age at diagnosis, sex and cohort. In LT-FH++/ADuLT those variables alter thresholds; in base PA-FGRS they alter a censored control's mixture weight through K_i. They do not alter h² or genetic correlations. Follow-up/censoring must be represented by a defensible observation model; independent censoring is required for ordinary Kaplan–Meier risk estimates, and with competing death the thresholds need a deliberate choice between net and crude incidence (the estimand choice). The PA-FGRS censored-control mixture inherits both requirements: its weight (K_pop − K_i)/K_pop reads a future case's not-yet-onset probability off the stratum's population CIP, which assumes censoring is non-informative given the stratum and onset timing among future cases independent of liability (see algorithm.md). When that independence fails (liability-dependent onset, ρ = 0.6), the mixture still leaves ranking intact and shifts calibration the way it is supposed to; it is the pinned case encoding that then over-conditions (RESULTS.md §16).

Gibbs targets the truncated-Gaussian conditional moments by Monte Carlo. PA is a deterministic sequential-moment approximation when several interval observations are folded in (exact for one truncation or point conditioning), so unusual family structures should be checked against Gibbs.

Shared household/cultural transmission, dominance/epistasis, indirect genetic effects and generative assortative mating are not included. Assortative mating is not an environmental component: it changes genetic covariances among mates and descendants. A directional maternal effect is likewise not generally represented by a symmetric shared-environment matrix. When omitted processes contribute to familial aggregation, read the output as the additive-model projection of the family history, not a pure causal genetic value.

PA can operate on a symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance when its non-deterministic interval coordinates are linearly independent after pin conditioning. Dependent intervals on singular support are rejected, including compatible ones: sequential moment projection cannot enforce that support. Singular target or unobserved rows alone are permitted. In contrast, gibbs_params and rtmvnorm_gibbs require a strictly positive-definite covariance so their conditional variances exist. Gibbs scoring supplements coordinate sweeps with joint Gaussian moves for strongly coupled blocks. Its batch-means SE still measures estimated sampling precision, not proof of stationarity; check difficult problems with independent seeds, longer burn-in/chains and a deterministic reference where available. The high-level estimators nudge a numerically singular assembled covariance to strict positive-definiteness and warn when they do so. Which entry points accept c2/m2 is listed under Scoring; multi-trait scoring is A+E only.

All common-threshold fitters require identifying contrasts among jointly observed phenotypes. Missing relatives cannot identify a component merely because the model can impute their liabilities. The joint fitter's re is the within-person residual E correlation; C/M correlations are separate. Omitting shared environment can distort the genetic/residual decomposition. These model components do not identify causal genetic or environmental effects.

The family-data fitters assume independent, non-overlapping families, and one of two sampling contracts. When members carry pid, a person who appears in more than one family is rejected rather than silently pooled. sampling="population" for an unascertained sample — screened for gross marginal inconsistency with your data, since the thresholds assert a prevalence the observed case rates should match. sampling="ipw" with per-family weights for a sample selected on observed status with a known, strictly positive inclusion probability (case/control cohorts, biobank case enrichment); see Inference.

Overlapping pedigrees invalidate the iid-family moments, and bootstrap does not correct selection bias. Selection on family history can be reweighted only when the inclusion probability of every complete observed family pattern is known and strictly positive. A design assigning zero inclusion probability to some stratum cannot be corrected — ascertainment through an affected proband is the standard example, where inclusion probability is zero for unaffected probands.

docs.title: Real-data checklist
docs.text:
First pick a use (Getting started, Table 1): I family-history risk prediction (own status out; optional PGS afterwards), II a quantitative GWAS phenotype (own status in), or III architecture / relationships / aetiology from h², r_g, residual r_e and/or the CIP. Use III can skip pedigree scoring; where uses I and II part company is item 8 below.

Then, before running a production analysis:

  1. Validate the diagnosis and family-history source: case definition, reporting accuracy, missingness, follow-up, and participation/selection process.
  2. Obtain population-representative CIPs (cumulative incidence by age), ideally from a register or other representative source — not the logistic default and not an ascertained biobank sample.
  3. Stratify CIPs by sex, birth year/cohort, ancestry and calendar period where incidence differs. With independent right censoring and no competing events, 1 − Kaplan–Meier estimates risk; with competing death or diagnoses, Aalen–Johansen gives the crude curve and Kaplan–Meier with those events censored the net curve; decide which the thresholds need (the estimand choice).
  4. Make each CIP age grid cover the analysed onset/follow-up ages and supply k_pop explicitly unless its final value is a defensible lifetime prevalence; the helper holds endpoint values constant outside the grid.
  5. Convert h² to the liability scale (observed_to_liability_h2), passing the actual study case fraction as prop_cases — the ascertainment correction matters for anything but a representative sample.
  6. Check sensitivity of the score to h² and to prevalence/CIP choices, especially for rare traits and dense pedigrees.
  7. Validate roles: valid abbreviations, no duplicate roles within a family (the estimator raises on duplicates).
  8. Decide whether to condition on the proband's own status. Include o for use II (a diagnosis-derived GWAS phenotype); for use I (prospective prediction/classification of that diagnosis) keep o and its pid with uninformative (-inf, inf) bounds (omitting o is allowed only when no member carries a pid).
  9. Decide case encoding — onset-pinned (thresholds_from_cip, case_mode="pin"), lifetime-interval (base PA-FGRS), or age-specific interval (case_mode="interval"; with the mixture, an age-dependent PA-FGRS-style variant) — and record it. Pin only when you believe onset is the CIP inverse of liability; under partial or noisy onset dependence the pin over-conditions and the lifetime interval is the safer encoding (RESULTS.md §16). The age-specific interval [T(onset), ∞) keeps most of the pin's ranking gain (§3) but over-disperses calibration (slope ≈ 0.83, §16).
  10. Choose Gibbs vs Pearson–Aitken; for unusual no-mixture pedigrees cross-check PA against Gibbs. The PA-FGRS censoring mixture has no Gibbs implementation.
  11. Residualize the phenotype for covariates (sex, cohort, PCs, batch). Prefer non-overlapping target families; if related targets remain, use and validate an association method that handles their relatedness, shared family-history phenotype, case-control imbalance, and tail behaviour (Zhuang et al. 2022).
  12. For built-in family-data fitting or bootstrap inference, require independent, non-overlapping families (a pid that appears in more than one family is rejected), and match the contract to the design: sampling="population" for an unascertained sample, or sampling="ipw" with weights = 1 / P(family sampled) when selection was on observed status with a known positive probability for every stratum. Check that your observed case rates plausibly match the prevalence behind your thresholds. The fitter raises only on gross mismatch (about 1.67× at K = 0.05 with 1,500 families), and a match does not prove joint-pattern positivity. A mismatch may equally mean the prevalence is wrong rather than the sample selected. Neither contract covers proband-ascertained families; those need an estimator that models the selection.
  13. For joint covariance fitting, supply one common case/control threshold per trait, model defensible shared-environment components, and inspect inference_status. Family-cluster SEs condition on the thresholds and weights; any covariance boundary withholds normal SEs. Missingness must preserve the modelled pair distributions, and zero-variance correlations are undefined. See the joint inference contract.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• h² must be liability-scale. Convert observed-scale estimates first.
  • Ages mean different things by status. For thresholds_from_cip, age_thresholds and pa_thresholds, age is the age of onset for cases and the age at last follow-up for controls.
  • Number repeated relatives (s1, s2) — an unnumbered duplicate role collides.
  • The proband's optional observed-status role is o, not g. g (what you estimate) is added for you.
  • Prevalence and CIPs should match the population the thresholds refer to; stratify by sex/birth-year if your incidence differs across strata (one CIP per stratum when building the bounds with thresholds_from_cip; the per-person K_i matters only for the PA mixture, use_mixture=True).
  • use_mixture=True needs K_i/K_pop on the members (from pa_thresholds or thresholds_from_cip) — otherwise it raises. In mixture mode, age enters through K_i; the implementation splits at the lifetime threshold and uses the finite control bound only as a censoring flag, so an age-specific control bound from these helpers is not applied twice. Their age-specific case bounds (pins or intervals) nevertheless remain a variant of base PA-FGRS.
  • Missing or uninformative family observations leave less conditioning information. If o is included, the estimate then relies mostly on the proband's own status; if o is also unbound, it shrinks toward the prior mean. Low prevalence alone does not imply little information: an affected person with a rare disease can be highly informative.
  • Install [fast] (Numba) for large runs; the pure-Python fallback is numerically identical but much slower.

docs.title: Estimating cumulative incidence (CIP) from health data
docs.text:
LT-FH++, ADuLT and PA-FGRS consume cumulative incidence—the population fraction diagnosed by a given age:

CIP(age | stratum) = P(diagnosed at or before age),   T = Phi^-1(1 - CIP).

The curve can be the analysis result itself or an input to thresholds. If a suitable published curve exists, skip to data preparation. This page estimates one from follow-up records.

docs.title: Input: follow-up records
docs.text:
Every estimator takes aligned 1-D arrays:

array meaning examples age_entry start of follow-up birth, register start, immigration, minimum onset age age_exit end of follow-up diagnosis, death, emigration, administrative end event code exit reason 0 censored, 1 diagnosis, 2 death or another competing event

Age is the time scale; calendar effects enter through entry/exit ages and stratification. A person is at risk at t when age_entry < t <= age_exit. Delayed entry therefore contributes risk only after entry. Entry and censoring must be non-informative conditional on modelled strata, with overlapping risk-set support. Ties are grouped by exit age. exit < entry and non-finite ages raise; zero-length follow-up contributes no risk and cannot carry an event.

For kaplan_meier_cip, the event array is boolean or exact 0/1. For aalen_johansen_cip, it is an integer code: 0 censored, cause (default 1) the target event, and other positive codes competing events.

docs.title: Kaplan-Meier (kaplan_meier_cip)
docs.text:
At each unique event age t_j, let d_j be target events and Y_j the number at risk:

S(t) = prod_{t_j <= t} (1 - d_j / Y_j),        CIP(t) = 1 - S(t)
Var(S(t)) = S(t)^2 * sum_{t_j <= t} d_j / (Y_j (Y_j - d_j)) .

Under independent censoring this estimates net risk in a hypothetical world without that censoring process. For the proportion actually diagnosed before death, death is a competing event, not ordinary censoring—even when death and diagnosis times are independent. Censoring the dead generally overestimates crude diagnosed incidence; use Aalen–Johansen instead.

docs.title: Aalen-Johansen (aalen_johansen_cip)
docs.text:
Let d_j count events of any type, d_kj events of cause k, and S overall event-free survival:

S(t) = prod_{t_j <= t} (1 - d_j / Y_j),
F_k(t) = sum_{t_j <= t} S(t_j-) * d_kj / Y_j .

F_k is crude cumulative incidence in the presence of competing events. Published LT-FH++ used this approach per sex and birth-year stratum with death and emigration as competing events.

Pointwise SEs use the finite-risk-set, tie-correct Aalen (1978) variance, in the grouped recurrence used by cmprsk::cuminc. At age t_j, for cause group r (target or all other causes), define

q_rj = 1                                   if d_rj = 1
        1 - (d_rj - 1) / (Y_j - 1)         otherwise,       (Equation 1)
a_rj = S(t_j-)^2 q_rj d_rj / Y_j^2 .                       (Equation 2)

For competing groups use u = F_k(t_j) / S_j+; for target events use u = 1 + F_k(t_j) / S_j+; both use w = 1 / S_j+. Update three running sums:

v1 <- v1 + u^2 a_rj
v2 <- v2 + w u a_rj
v3 <- v3 + w^2 a_rj,                                      (Equation 3)
Var F_k(t_j) = v1 + F_k(t_j)^2 v3 - 2 F_k(t_j) v2.         (Equation 4)

Competing-group updates are skipped when S_j+ = 0; target events use the removable boundary w = 0, u = 1. Separate cause/other updates are essential for tied causes. With one event type, Aalen and Greenwood variances agree asymptotically, not as finite-sample identities.

docs.title: The estimand choice (the most important decision on this page)
docs.text:
• Net incidence (1 - Kaplan–Meier, death censored): incidence in a hypothetical no-death world, not usually the registry's diagnosed proportion.
  • Crude incidence (Aalen–Johansen): probability of diagnosis by age t in the real population with competing death. This is the published LT-FH++ convention; thresholds_from_cip accepts either curve.
  • Plain age-specific proportions: appropriate only with essentially complete follow-up beyond the target age. Recent, right-censored cohorts undercount late onset.

Threshold choice is also a model decision. If death is independent of liability, threshold crossing among people alive at t implies the net curve. If death is liability-related, or the target is the population diagnosed fraction, the crude curve is natural. They differ little when death before onset is rare. The end-to-end example used net incidence without mortality; Aalen–Johansen thresholds with mortality remain untested.

benchmarks/bench_cip_estimation.py reports AJ recovery to about 0.002 absolute error at N = 50,000 and KM-as-censoring overshoot up to 0.022 at a 42% death share in its simulated registry.

docs.title: Stratification
docs.text:
Estimate one curve per population stratum (published LT-FH++ used sex × birth year):

import numpy as np
from ltpred import aalen_johansen_cip, thresholds_from_cip

# event: 0 censored, 1 diagnosis, 2 death
stratum = np.char.add(sex.astype(str), birth_year.astype(str))
lower = np.empty(len(status))
upper = np.empty(len(status))
for key in np.unique(stratum):
    m = stratum == key
    curve = aalen_johansen_cip(age_entry[m], age_exit[m], event[m])
    ages = np.r_[0.0, curve.ages]       # anchor at (0, 0)
    values = np.r_[0.0, curve.values]
    lower[m], upper[m], _, _ = thresholds_from_cip(
        status[m], age[m], ages, values)

Sparse strata produce noisy step curves; pooling adjacent birth years trades resolution for stability. curve.n_events and curve.se expose sparsity. A stratum with no events raises. thresholds_from_cip defaults k_pop to the curve maximum, which is lifetime prevalence only if the curve reaches that horizon; otherwise supply it from an older stratum or literature.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from ltpred import aalen_johansen_cip

entry = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 5, 10, 0, 0])
exit_ = np.array([40, 52, 47, 60, 55, 61, 44, 57])
event = np.array([1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1])

diag = aalen_johansen_cip(entry, exit_, event)
death = aalen_johansen_cip(entry, exit_, event, cause=2)
age at risk Y event F_diag F_death 40 8 diag 0.125 0.000 47 6 diag 0.271 0.000 52 5 death 0.271 0.146 55 4 diag 0.417 0.146 57 3 diag 0.563 0.146 61 1 death 0.563 0.438

At 40, one diagnosis among eight gives S = 7/8 and F_diag = 1/8. At 47, the diagnosis and a censoring have left, so F_diag = 0.125 + (7/8)(1/6) = 0.271. At 52, death adds (7/8)(5/6)(1/5) = 0.146 to F_death only. At the horizon, F_diag + F_death = 1 - S, as required.

docs.title: Edge cases and gotchas
docs.text:
• Prevalent cases: exclude diagnoses before entry; they are not incident.
  • Zero-length follow-up: censored rows contribute nothing; event-coded rows raise because no one was at risk.
  • Beyond the event grid: incidence is not extrapolated. thresholds_from_cip holds the last value constant. Prepend (0, 0) as above or younger rows use the first event age's incidence.
  • Zero incidence: values are clipped to [min_cip, k_pop] (default min_cip=1e-5), which can put an onset in a zero-CIP region at an arbitrary high threshold.
  • CIP exactly one: valid when the last target event exhausts the risk set, but no finite probit threshold exists. Choose a justified earlier/lifetime horizon.
  • Emigration: ordinary censoring under the liability model; LT-FH++ coded it as competing. Keep death as a separate event so net and crude curves can both be formed.
  • Uncertainty: returned SEs diagnose curve precision; they are not propagated into thresholds.

docs.title: Validation and references
docs.text:
tests/test_cip.py checks hand-computed KM/AJ curves, delayed entry, Greenwood and tied finite-risk Aalen variances, exhausted risk sets and threshold integration. benchmarks/bench_cip_estimation.py measures curve recovery, competing-risk bias and end-to-end scoring.

  • Pedersen et al. (2022), Am J Hum Genet — LT-FH++ and its AJ curves (10.1016/j.ajhg.2022.01.009).
  • Andersen, Borgan, Gill & Keiding (1993), Statistical Models Based on Counting Processes — risk sets and AJ variance (sec. IV.4).
  • Aalen (1978), Ann Statist 6:534-545 — CIF variance.
  • Beck et al. (2024), Acta Psychiatr Scand — delayed entry and competing risks (PMC11065580).
  • Greenwood (1926), Kaplan & Meier (1958) — variance and product-limit estimator.

docs.title: Data preparation
docs.text: Turn status, age and relationships into liability bounds and families. For a first run see Getting started or the register tutorial.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Use one row per observed person, grouped by target proband:

column meaning fam_id family/proband group role relationship to the proband lower, upper liability interval, derived from status and optionally age pid (optional) personal identifier K_i, K_pop (optional) current and lifetime incidence for the PA mixture

Do not supply genetic role g; the estimator adds and returns that coordinate.

docs.title: Role grammar
docs.text:
role who o (optional) proband's own status m, f mother, father s, s1, s2, … full sibling(s); number repeated roles mgm, mgf, pgm, pgf maternal/paternal grandparents mhs1…, phs1… maternal/paternal half-siblings mau1…, pau1… maternal/paternal aunts/uncles c1.1, c1.2, … children (partner-group . child index)

Any subset is allowed. Duplicate roles raise. With no personal ids, missing o is inserted as uninformative. With pids, retain o and its pid even when its bounds are (-inf, inf). Include own diagnosis for a GWAS; leave it uninformative for prediction and censor relatives at the landmark.

Same-side half-sib sets (mhs1/mhs2 or phs1/phs2) follow LTFHPlus's shared-other-parent convention and are related 0.5·h² to each other, not 0.25·h². If their other parents differ, the role grammar cannot represent that: use a pedigree matrix instead.

docs.title: Beyond the role grammar: arbitrary pedigrees
docs.text:
For population parent-pointer data, use estimate_liabilities. It discovers each proband's pedigree, applies CIP bounds and scores in one call:

from ltpred import estimate_liabilities

gwas_scores = estimate_liabilities(
    ids, father, mother, probands=gwas_ids, status=status, age=age,
    use="gwas", strata=stratum, cip_by_stratum=cip_by_stratum,
    max_degree=3, h2=0.5)

prediction_scores = estimate_liabilities(
    ids, father, mother, probands=prediction_ids, status=status, age=age,
    use="prediction", birth_time=birth_time, index_time=index_time,
    strata=stratum, cip_by_stratum=cip_by_stratum,
    max_degree=3, h2=0.5)

birth_time and strata align to ids; index_time aligns to probands. Their calendar unit must match age. At landmark t, a relative born at b is censored at age t - b; people not yet born are uninformative. Only proband_state == "disease_free_and_followed" belongs in a prospective incident-risk evaluation.

Pedigree extraction includes every recorded ancestor needed for exact kinship. Ancestors beyond max_degree are marked closure_only and their diagnoses are ignored unless condition_closure=True. Unlisted parents are founders, but frac_records_with_unresolved_parents exposes a likely register boundary or broken join; no resolved non-null parent reference raises. This driver uses pinned-onset LT-FH++ and PA. Other observation models use the lower-level APIs.

For deeper pedigrees, cousins, multiple marriages or inbreeding, construct the additive matrix directly:

from ltpred import kinship_from_pedigree, estimate_liability_from_kinship

ids    = ["o", "m", "f", "s1", "mgm", "mgf"]      # target first
father = ["f", "mgf", None, "f", None, None]      # None / unlisted = founder
mother = ["m", "mgm", None, "m", None, None]
_, A = kinship_from_pedigree(ids, father, mother)
# lower/upper: (n_families, n_individuals), aligned to ids
gen, se, var = estimate_liability_from_kinship(A, lower, upper, h2=0.5, target=0)

PA is the default; use method="gibbs" for a sampler-based SE. var is posterior variance on both. The PA-only mixture accepts aligned K_i/K_pop. C/M scoring requires explicit aligned c_kernel/m_kernel matrices because those environmental classes cannot be recovered from A. Inbred full liabilities are standardised to unit variance, preserving the threshold scale. construct_covmat_from_kinship exposes the covariance alone.

Role and pedigree paths agree when they encode the same relationships (apart from the half-sib convention above and PA fold order). The graph-extraction approach follows Pedersen et al. 2025. Do not pass LTFHPlus get_kinship output directly: ltpred expects the unscaled A = 2φ and applies h2 itself.

docs.title: Getting lower/upper from status and age
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from ltpred import prevalence_thresholds, age_thresholds, pa_thresholds

status = np.array([1, 0, 1, 0])          # 1 = case
age    = np.array([45, 70, 52, 33])      # onset for cases, last follow-up for controls

lower, upper = prevalence_thresholds(status, pop_prev=0.05)
lower, upper = age_thresholds(status, age, pop_prev=0.05)
lower, upper, K_i, K_pop = pa_thresholds(status, age, pop_prev=0.05)
builder cases controls outputs and scope prevalence_thresholds (T, ∞) (-∞, T) bounds; classic LT-FH age_thresholds pinned at T(onset) (-∞, T(age)) bounds; logistic demonstration pa_thresholds (T(onset), ∞) (-∞, T(age)) bounds plus K_i, K_pop; age-dependent PA-FGRS-style variant

Here T = Φ⁻¹(1 − K). Personalised bounds with relatives define LT-FH++; with role o only they define ADuLT. Pins assume a deterministic monotone onset–liability map and can over-condition noisy diagnosis ages. Intervals make a weaker assumption but are not automatically more conservative.

Base PA-FGRS is different: cases use the lifetime threshold and age enters only the control mixture. Construct lifetime bounds and control mixture data separately:

from ltpred import estimate_liability, families_from_columns, pa_thresholds, prevalence_thresholds

lower, upper = prevalence_thresholds(status, pop_prev=0.05)
_, _, K_i, K_pop = pa_thresholds(status, age, pop_prev=0.05)

# For prediction, copy the arrays and set the proband's bounds to (-inf, inf)
# and K_i/K_pop to NaN. For a GWAS, include the proband's diagnosis.
res = estimate_liability(
    families_from_columns(fam_id=fam_id, role=role, lower=lower, upper=upper,
                          K_i=K_i, K_pop=K_pop),
    h2=0.5, use_mixture=True)

For real data, obtain K_i from an appropriate population CIP rather than the logistic demo. Any explicit interval is also valid: lower == upper is a pin and (-inf, inf) is uninformative.

CIPs and sex/cohort. There is no sex argument. Sex, birth year and cohort enter personalised thresholds, or base PA-FGRS mixture weights through K_i; they do not change covariance. Use population-representative curves, not CIPs estimated from an ascertained biobank sample. The choice between net and competing-risk incidence is an estimand decision.

thresholds_from_cip interpolates within its age grid and holds endpoint values constant outside it. Cover all analysed ages. Its default k_pop = max(cip_values) is appropriate only when the curve reaches the intended lifetime horizon; otherwise supply k_pop explicitly.

docs.title: Estimating the CIP from follow-up records
docs.text:
ltpred.cip implements Kaplan–Meier and Aalen–Johansen estimation with delayed entry and right censoring:

from ltpred import aalen_johansen_cip, kaplan_meier_cip

# age_entry/age_exit per person; event: 0 censoring, 1 diagnosis, 2 death
curve = aalen_johansen_cip(age_entry, age_exit, event_type)

Call once per population stratum, then feed curve.ages and curve.values to thresholds_from_cip. An exact terminal CIP of one has no finite probit threshold. CIP estimation owns the risk sets, equations, variance estimators and examples.

docs.title: A real register-data recipe
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from ltpred import thresholds_from_cip, families_from_columns, estimate_liability

# One stratum label per observed member row; each value is
# (CIP ages, CIP values, lifetime prevalence).
stratum = np.asarray(sex_birth_cohort_ancestry)
cip_by_stratum = {
    "F_1950_EUR": (ages_f50, cip_f50, lifetime_f50),
    "M_1950_EUR": (ages_m50, cip_m50, lifetime_m50),
}
status, age = np.asarray(status), np.asarray(age)
lower = np.empty(status.shape, dtype=float)
upper = np.empty(status.shape, dtype=float)
K_i = np.full(status.shape, np.nan)
K_pop = np.full(status.shape, np.nan)

case_mode = "pin"  # or "interval" for the age-dependent PA-style variant
for label in np.unique(stratum):
    mask = stratum == label
    cip_ages, cip_values, lifetime_prevalence = cip_by_stratum[label]
    lo, hi, ki, kp = thresholds_from_cip(
        status[mask], age[mask], cip_ages, cip_values,
        k_pop=lifetime_prevalence, case_mode=case_mode)
    lower[mask], upper[mask] = lo, hi
    K_i[mask], K_pop[mask] = ki, kp

families = families_from_columns(
    fam_id, role, lower, upper, pid=pid, K_i=K_i, K_pop=K_pop)
res = estimate_liability(
    families, h2=0.5, use_mixture=(case_mode == "interval"))

case_mode="pin" is onset-pinned LT-FH++/ADuLT. "interval" with the mixture is the age-dependent PA-FGRS-style variant, not base PA-FGRS or PA-FGRS_ADT. Mixture input is PA-only and requires valid control K pairs. For ADuLT, use the same personalised bounds but only role o; there is no separate engine switch.

docs.title: Getting heritability on the liability scale
docs.text:
Convert observed-scale estimates with the study's actual case fraction:

from ltpred import observed_to_liability_h2

study_case_fraction = n_cases / sample_size
h2_liab = observed_to_liability_h2(
    obs_h2=0.15, pop_prev=0.05, prop_cases=study_case_fraction)

Omit prop_cases only for a population-representative sample. The related helpers provide the inverse bridge and probit variance q = 2 f (1-f) beta². Sum independent/LD-pruned q values before converting to total-liability fraction q/(1+q).

Use the additive variance component you want the family covariance to represent. Pedigree/twin narrow-sense estimates capture more family signal but can include unmodelled shared or indirect effects; SNP heritability is usually a conservative lower bound for the h²·A covariance. Run sensitivity analyses over plausible h² and CIP values (example). When the sampling contract holds, fit h² from the families. Tetrachoric relative-pair correlations are a fitting-free diagnostic:

from ltpred import tetrachoric
r = tetrachoric(proband_status, mother_status)
h2_falconer = 2 * r.rho       # parent–offspring, additive A+E model

That shortcut assumes population sampling, age-complete statuses and no shared or transmitted environment. Compare pairwise estimates with the h² × A covariance you intend to use.

docs.title: Preparing multiple traits for covariance fitting
docs.text:
Use independent role families and one common prevalence per trait. Missing phenotypes are NaN in the status matrix and remain (-inf, inf) bounds—not controls:

import numpy as np
from ltpred import families_from_columns, prevalence_thresholds

# status: (n_people, n_traits); prevalence: one value per trait
lower = np.full(status.shape, -np.inf)
upper = np.full(status.shape, np.inf)
for p, k in enumerate(prevalence):
    observed = ~np.isnan(status[:, p])
    lower[observed, p], upper[observed, p] = prevalence_thresholds(
        status[observed, p], pop_prev=k)
two_trait_families = families_from_columns(fam_id, role, lower, upper, pid=pid)

Keep phen_names in trait-column order and IPW weights in first-appearance family order. Personalised CIP/onset bounds are rejected by this fitter. Identification uses jointly observed pairs; entirely missing relatives add no information and dropping missingness does not correct informative missingness. See joint inference and the tutorial.

docs.title: Scoring genetic liabilities
docs.text: This page covers estimator choice, outputs and scaling. Build bounds first with data preparation; the model reference defines the estimand.

docs.title: Choose a scoring model
docs.text:
Table 1. Scoring paths by observation model.

use case records and bounds engine model no age, with relatives prevalence_thresholds; identified o plus relatives PA or Gibbs classic LT-FH additive, noninbred nuclear family roles o/m/f/s1/s2/…; no C/M or mixture; 0 <= h2 < 1 quadrature numerical cross-check of the same posterior personalised CIP, with relatives thresholds_from_cip(…, case_mode="pin") PA (default) or Gibbs LT-FH++ personalised CIP, no relatives the same bounds for role o only PA (default) or Gibbs ADuLT logistic demonstration age_thresholds PA or Gibbs age-only demonstration population register estimate_liabilities(…, use="gwas" or "prediction") PA pinned-onset LT-FH++ arbitrary pedigree kinship_from_pedigree + estimate_liability_from_kinship PA or Gibbs LT-FH / LT-FH++ base PA-FGRS lifetime bounds from prevalence_thresholds; control-specific K_i/K_pop PA with use_mixture=True PA-FGRS age-dependent interval/mixture encoding pa_thresholds or thresholds_from_cip(…, case_mode="interval") PA with use_mixture=True PA-FGRS-style variant multiple traits vector h2, genetic and full-liability correlation matrices Gibbs A+E covariance

In base PA-FGRS, every observed case uses [Φ⁻¹(1 − K_pop), ∞). Age-specific incidence enters the censored-control mixture, not the case threshold. The convenience interval helpers instead put cases above their onset threshold. That is a different observation model, not base PA-FGRS or a faithful PA-FGRS_ADT implementation; see the explicit base recipe.

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
from ltpred import families_from_columns, estimate_liability

families = families_from_columns(
    fam_id=fam_id, role=role, lower=lower, upper=upper,
    pid=pid,                    # optional personal join keys
    # K_i=K_i, K_pop=K_pop,     # PA mixture only
)
res = estimate_liability(families, h2=0.5, out=("genetic",))
score = res.genetic             # shorthand for res.est["genetic"]

Rows sharing a fam_id become one family. Include role o with its diagnosis for a GWAS phenotype. For prediction, retain o and its pid but use (-inf, inf) bounds. Only wholly pid-free families may omit that row and fall back to fam_id as the result key. An identified relative without an identified proband raises rather than silently losing the join.

Single-trait estimation defaults to deterministic Pearson–Aitken (PA); multi-trait estimation defaults to Gibbs. Use method="gibbs" for a sampling cross-check or Monte-Carlo SE, "pa" to force PA, and "quadrature" for the restricted numerical integration route. dtype=np.float32 halves bound storage while accumulators remain float64. The options reference collects the remaining controls.

docs.title: Reading LiabilityResult
docs.text:
Table 2. Estimates and numerical diagnostics.

field meaning res.fam_ids, res.pids family ids and proband join keys, aligned to input families res.est["genetic"] posterior-mean genetic-liability score res.est["full"] full-liability estimate, if requested res.se["genetic"] Gibbs batch-means Monte-Carlo SE; zero for deterministic PA and quadrature res.var["genetic"] posterior conditional variance, not an SE that shrinks with numerical effort res.quadrature_error[...] largest mean/variance change over the last two refinements; not an error bound res.quadrature_nodes[...] nodes per active factor dimension; zero for an analytic answer

var describes uncertainty about the proband, se describes sampling noise, and quadrature_error describes grid refinement. Zero deterministic se does not imply zero approximation or integration error. Multi-trait columns are suffixed by phenotype, for example res.est["genetic_height"].

res.to_dict() copies aligned estimate and diagnostic columns; res.to_frame() returns them as a pandas DataFrame (pandas is optional). Repeated pids remain separate rows, so validate join cardinality. PopulationScores and QuadratureResult provide the same export pattern. Array tuple APIs return PA (est, var), Gibbs (est, se) or (est, se, var) with return_var=True, and kinship (est, se, var).

out="full" means E[l_o | own interval and relatives]. PA conditions exact pins first and folds an unpinned target's interval after the remaining relative intervals. The usual GWAS phenotype is still out="genetic".

docs.title: What the score is — and is not
docs.text:
The target is the model-defined posterior mean additive genetic liability:

mu_i = E[a_i | statuses, ages, family structure, h2, CIP/prevalence model]

It is a latent, standardised-liability phenotype—the family-history analogue of a BLUP or selection-index breeding value—not a SNP polygenic score or an absolute disease risk. Scoring conditions on h2, prevalence/CIPs and family covariance; it does not estimate them as a side effect.

  • GWAS phenotype: include the proband's diagnosis. The resulting phenotype contains that diagnosis and is not a leakage-free predictor.
  • Family-history prediction: leave own status uninformative and censor every relative at the prediction landmark. A relative born at b is observed only to age t - b. Only estimate_liabilities(use="prediction") applies this calendar censoring for you.
  • Combining with a PGS: fit a separate downstream model in the target population; do not add uncalibrated scores. Existing studies report complementarity between family-history and SNP predictors (Hujoel et al. 2022, Dybdahl Krebs et al. 2026).

docs.title: Shared-environment components (C and M)
docs.text:
The default covariance is additive-genetic only. Optional full-sibship (C) and mate-pair (M) components prevent environmental resemblance from being attributed to the genetic target:

Cov(l_i, l_j) = h2 * A_ij + c2 * C_ij + m2 * M_ij   (i != j)
Var(l_i)      = h2 + c2 + m2 + e2 = 1

Thus h2 + c2 + m2 <= 1. The genetic target remains coupled to relatives only through h2 * A.

from ltpred import estimate_liability, fit_variance_components

fit = fit_variance_components(families, ("A", "C", "M"), sampling="population")
res = estimate_liability(
    families, h2=fit.components["A"],
    c2=fit.components.get("C", 0.0), m2=fit.components.get("M", 0.0))

Known values can be supplied directly. The role/object and single-trait array APIs accept c2/m2. The kinship route additionally requires aligned c_kernel/m_kernel matrices (finite, symmetric PSD, unit diagonal), because A cannot distinguish full siblings from parent–offspring or mates from strangers:

gen, se, var = estimate_liability_from_kinship(
    A, lower, upper, h2=0.4,
    c2=0.15, c_kernel=C, m2=0.10, m_kernel=M)

Component fitting requires independent, non-overlapping families, common thresholds and a declared sampling design. It is not a fitter for overlapping register pedigrees. For selected samples, sampling="ipw" is valid only with known, strictly positive inclusion probabilities for every complete observed family pattern; the family bootstrap does not correct ascertainment. See fitting and ascertainment.

docs.title: Choosing Gibbs vs Pearson–Aitken
docs.text:
Both engines target the same posterior mean. Gibbs is exact in the limit of infinite draws. No-mixture PA conditions pins jointly and marginalises uninformative rows first; it is exact with zero or one remaining interval and a sequential two-moment approximation otherwise. Its fold order is canonical (sorted roles) for reproducibility, not an accuracy guarantee.

Table 3. Inference engines.

Gibbs Pearson–Aitken method truncated-MVN Monte Carlo, with collapsed unbounded coordinates deterministic sequential moments error batch-means MC SE no MC error; approximation error outside exact cases posterior variance retained-draw estimate sequential-moment approximation exactness exact in the limit exact after pins with at most one interval censoring mixture not implemented use_mixture=True typical use multi-trait and sampling cross-checks single-trait production scoring

On benchmarked no-mixture structures, PA and Gibbs genetic estimates had correlation ≥ 0.997. Cross-check unusual, densely affected or heavily truncated pedigrees against Gibbs. Fold-order stress results and locked comparisons with LTFHPlus/LTFGRS are in RESULTS §§1, 2, 14 and 30. Those no-mixture comparisons do not validate the PA-only mixture. Hujoel et al.'s less favourable aggregate-sibling comparison used a union event rather than separately observed sibling intervals, so it is not the input model here (2020).

Use rtmvnorm_gibbs directly only when retained TMVN draws are required; the high-level estimator returns summaries. Batch means estimate MC precision, not a proof of stationarity: difficult bounds still warrant independent seeds and longer chains.

docs.title: Nuclear-family quadrature
docs.text:
For an additive, noninbred nuclear-family cross-check, use method="quadrature" or the explicit array API. Conditioning on the two parental breeding values leaves at most a two-dimensional integral; siblings add likelihood factors, not dimensions.

import numpy as np
from ltpred import estimate_liability_quadrature_arrays

q = estimate_liability_quadrature_arrays(
    roles=["o", "m", "f", "s1"],
    lower=[[2.0, -np.inf, 0.5, -np.inf]],
    upper=[[2.0, 1.5, np.inf, 1.5]],
    h2=0.5, out="genetic", atol=1e-8, max_nodes=128,
)
q.est, q.var              # posterior mean and variance
q.error, q.n_nodes        # refinement change and nodes per active dimension

Bounds have shape (n_families, len(roles)). Supported roles are unique o, m, f, s1, s2, … with unrelated, noninbred parents and 0 <= h2 < 1. C/M, mixtures and other pedigrees are unsupported. Leave o uninformative for relatives-only prediction.

Two successive refinements must meet atol; max_nodes is 64–512 per active dimension. Nonconvergence raises with the failing row (under the object API, its index within its role-set group). q.error is the larger of those changes, not a certified error bound. Analytic answers use zero nodes. The object API exposes the same diagnostics as quadrature_error and quadrature_nodes.

docs.title: Scaling to large cohorts
docs.text:
Array APIs avoid Family/Member objects and construct one covariance per role set:

from ltpred import estimate_liability_pa_arrays

est, var = estimate_liability_pa_arrays(
    roles=["o", "m", "f", "s1"], lower=lower, upper=upper, h2=0.5,
    out="genetic",                 # or use_mixture=True with K_i=, K_pop=
)

The warmed grid that shipped with v0.4.0 (four threads; benchmarks/bench_scaling.csv, commit 1684fc5) measured 13–29× faster than the object path at 2.02–6.29 million already-aligned families/s. It has not been re-measured; later object-path improvements make the current ratio smaller. estimate_liability_gibbs_arrays provides the corresponding Gibbs interface. Call ltpred.set_num_threads(n) to control Numba workers and warm the JIT before timing.

The chunked and batch drivers bound kernel working memory:

from ltpred import (estimate_liability_pa_chunked,
                    estimate_liability_pa_batches,
                    estimate_liability_gibbs_chunked)

est, var = estimate_liability_pa_chunked(
    roles, lower, upper, h2=0.5, chunk_size=65_536)
est, se = estimate_liability_gibbs_chunked(
    roles, lower, upper, h2=0.5, seed=1, chunk_size=4096)

est, var = estimate_liability_pa_batches(
    roles,
    ((lower_mm[i:i+65_536], upper_mm[i:i+65_536])
     for i in range(0, n_families, 65_536)),
    h2=0.5)

Gibbs seeds by global row position, so any chunking is bit-identical to the one-shot call. PA agrees to rounding. An in-memory chunked array still holds all bounds; use an iterator or memmap with *_batches to avoid that. Mixture validation is global for *_chunked and per batch for *_batches. estimate_liability_gibbs_batches uses the same global-row seed rule.

Shape and memory. lower and upper are (n_families, len(roles)) and column j matches roles[j]; g is added internally. Encode an absent or uninformative relative as lower[i,j] = -np.inf, upper[i,j] = np.inf, not as a control. Float32 bound/K arrays halve the cohort-scale input footprint while covariances, conditional factors and accumulators stay float64. Quantising the small shared covariance would save little and harm the solve.

PA does not modify inputs. Historical time/memory comparisons and their exact output checks are in RESULTS §31. For large simulated registers, simulate_register_liabilities(method="mendelian") avoids the dense relationship matrix and factorisation; it preserves the model, including inbreeding, but not dense-method seeded draws.

docs.title: Multiple correlated traits
docs.text:
import numpy as np
res = estimate_liability(
    families, h2=[0.5, 0.3],
    genetic_corrmat=np.array([[1, 0.4], [0.4, 1]]),
    full_corrmat=np.array([[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]),
    phen_names=["A", "B"], out=("genetic",))
res.est["genetic_A"], res.est["genetic_B"]

Every member needs one interval per trait. With D = diag(sqrt(h2)), both G = D @ genetic_corrmat @ D and full_corrmat - G must be PSD. Multi-trait scoring is Gibbs-only. Nonzero c2/m2 raises because proportions alone do not specify cross-trait environmental covariance.

For common-threshold data, fit_pairwise_multi jointly fits heritabilities and correlations. An A+E fit supplies joint.h2, joint.rg and joint.rp for the inputs above. A fit including C/M cannot be transferred to this A+E scorer; see joint inference.

docs.title: Using the estimate in a GWAS
docs.text:
Use the genetic estimate as a continuous phenotype. Join genotypes explicitly to res.pids, residualize the phenotype and adjust for sex, cohort, ancestry PCs, batch and design covariates, or use an appropriate linear mixed model. Prefer non-overlapping target families. If related targets remain, validate calibration under the actual relatedness, case-control imbalance and variant frequency spectrum; an ordinary LMM is not a blanket guarantee (Hujoel et al. 2020; Zhuang et al. 2022).

# Simple sketch after covariate residualization and checked pid alignment:
y = res.est["genetic"]
y = (y - y.mean()) / y.std()
chi2 = len(y) * ((Xs.T @ y) / len(y)) ** 2

In the replicated independent-SNP, non-overlapping-family benchmark, PA and Gibbs gave a 1.47 ± 0.04× causal-SNP noncentrality ratio over case/control. That is not the squared-correlation effective-N proxy or a real-LD, relatedness-aware mixed-model result. Cohort-specific thresholds removed the inflation in one secular-trend simulation; they do not replace ordinary GWAS covariate adjustment. See RESULTS §§4 and 13.

docs.text:
Table 5. Migration equivalents.

R ltpred estimate_liability(.tbl = df, …) families_from_columns(...), then estimate_liability(families, h2=…) column-name arguments pass the columns themselves $genetic_est res.genetic LTFGRS PA $var res.var["genetic"], not res.se (zero under deterministic PA) future::plan(multisession, workers = n) ltpred.set_num_threads(n)

Role labels are unchanged except children: write c<group>.<idx>; children in different partner groups are half sibs. ltpred ships no igraph-style pedigree object or plotting utilities.

docs.title: Fitting model parameters
docs.text:
Fit liability-scale heritability, genetic/residual correlations and shared-environment covariance from family data. If those parameters are already available, go to Scoring. Unsupported prototypes stay in research extensions.

Supported sampling contract

All four fitters assume independent, non-overlapping families and common case/control thresholds. When pid is supplied, a person appearing in more than one family raises. Use estimate_liability for overlapping register pedigrees.

Use sampling="population" for an unascertained sample. For selection on observed status, use sampling="ipw" with one reciprocal known, strictly positive inclusion probability per family. Omitting sampling warns and assumes population sampling. No weight can reconstruct a stratum with zero inclusion probability, and bootstrap_fit does not repair selection bias.

Under population sampling, each role's case rate is screened for gross inconsistency with the threshold's prevalence. A mismatch can mean ascertainment or the wrong prevalence. The screen is not a certificate: at K = 0.05 its detectable enrichment is about 1.67× at N = 1,500 and 1.26× at N = 10,000, with a 1.15× floor binding at large N. The benchmark shows 1.51× enrichment already inflates h² by +0.48.

Under IPW, a large weighted mismatch only warns. Its trigger uses Kish effective sample size as an uncalibrated heuristic, not a binomial test: outcome-dependent weights change the sampling variance. Sampled weights alone cannot establish that a design is invalid or a stratum has zero inclusion probability.

The meaning of se differs by method. Haseman–Elston (HE) fits report a within-dataset Monte-Carlo diagnostic, not sampling uncertainty. Pairwise fits report conditional, asymptotic family-cluster sampling SEs for identifiable interior estimates. bootstrap_fit provides approximate family-cluster uncertainty when its design assumptions hold.

docs.title: Choose a fitter
docs.text:
Table 1. Fitters for independent families with common binary thresholds.

fitter use when computation and uncertainty fit_heritability additive h² only stochastic moment fixed point; family bootstrap fit_variance_components separate A, C and/or M with identifying relationships stochastic moment fixed point; family bootstrap fit_pairwise deterministic single-trait A/C/M composite likelihood; interior cluster-sandwich SEs fit_pairwise_multi joint trait h², genetic/residual correlations, optional C/M multivariate composite likelihood; interior cluster/delta-method SEs

Personalised CIP/onset bounds are for scoring, not these fits. Identification requires jointly observed relationship contrasts. The stochastic fitters are one to two orders of magnitude slower at their defaults; shortening their Gibbs schedules requires separate Monte Carlo checks. See the benchmark ledger for measured recovery and cost.

docs.title: Fitting heritability from the family data
docs.text:
fit_heritability alternates Gibbs augmentation of latent liabilities with a damped Haseman–Elston update. This is a stochastic-approximation fixed point, not posterior sampling: the trace is not a posterior chain and its mean is not a posterior mean.

from ltpred import fit_heritability
fit = fit_heritability(fitting_families, sampling="population")
fit.h2, fit.h2_se       # estimate and within-fit MC diagnostic

Relatives are required. fit.h2_se is not an inferential SE and understated across-dataset variability in benchmarks; use bootstrap_fit for that. The fitter requires one common threshold per trait and rejects personalised bounds, onset pins and two-sided intervals. That is the validated implementation scope, not evidence that heterogeneous thresholds invalidate the moment identity. estimate_liability still accepts personalised bounds because it conditions on h2 rather than fitting it.

docs.title: Family-cluster uncertainty: bootstrap_fit
docs.text:
from ltpred import bootstrap_fit
bs = bootstrap_fit(
    families,
    lambda f: fit_heritability(f, seed=1, sampling="population").h2,
    n_boot=100,
)
bs.estimate, bs.se, (bs.ci_low, bs.ci_high)

The callback can return any scalar or array from a fitter. Fix its internal seed so spread reflects family resampling rather than sampler noise. For IPW, pass weights=weights and use a two-argument callback such as lambda f, w: fit_heritability(f, sampling="ipw", weights=w, seed=1).h2; families and weights are resampled by the same indices.

Cost is n_boot + 1 fits. The interval assumes independent clusters and a valid sampling design; zero-probability strata, overlapping pedigrees and boundary parameters need separate treatment. Increase n_boot until the SE and percentile endpoints are stable and report the value used.

docs.title: Deterministic pairwise fitting
docs.text:
fit_pairwise estimates the same A/C/M fractions from binary relative-pair probabilities without sampling latent liabilities:

from ltpred import fit_pairwise
pw = fit_pairwise(fitting_families, components=("A", "C"), sampling="population")
pw.components, pw.residual
pw.se, pw.inference_status

Components need independent identifying contrasts among observed pairs. Fractions are nonnegative and sum to at most 1 - eps (1e-6 by default). Failed, infeasible or nonstationary optimization raises. IPW weights are normalised to mean one; the weighted marginal screen does not prove joint positivity or weight correctness.

For an interior fit, pw.covariance follows pw.component_order and pw.se is its diagonal SD. The sandwich uses family-level score variation, so pairs sharing a member are not treated as independent. It is conditional on supplied thresholds and weights and is asymptotic, not a finite-sample calibration claim. At a component/residual boundary (within max(1e-7, 10*tol)), at_boundary is true and covariance/SEs are NaN; inference_status also distinguishes insufficient clusters or information. Ordinary normal intervals and likelihood-ratio tests are then inappropriate. Bootstrap/profile inference at a boundary needs its own calibration.

docs.title: Joint heritability and cross-trait correlations
docs.text:
from ltpred import fit_pairwise_multi
joint = fit_pairwise_multi(
    two_trait_families, components=("A", "C", "M"), sampling="population")
joint.h2, joint.rg, joint.re
joint.se["h2"], joint.se["rg"], joint.se["re"]
joint.components["C"], joint.correlations["C"]
joint.inference_status

Each member needs one bound per trait. Thresholds may differ between traits but must be common across people within each trait. Missing phenotypes use (-inf, inf); see the input recipe.

With phenotype-major coordinates, the fitted model is

\[ \Sigma = G\otimes A + S\otimes C + T\otimes M + E\otimes I, \qquad \operatorname{diag}(G+S+T+E)=1. \tag{1} \]

components=("A",) omits S and T. Every component is PSD and residual E has eigenvalues at least eps. C means full-sibship environment; M describes spousal resemblance, not the inheritance consequences of assortative mating.

h2 = diag(G), rg standardises G and re standardises residual E. Shared-environment correlations are separate in correlations["C"] and correlations["M"]. rp sums all components, so rp - genetic_cov is total non-genetic covariance and differs from env_cov when C/M is present. These are model decompositions, not causal effects.

Only jointly observed coordinates contribute. Missingness must preserve pair distributions; imputing a completely missing relative creates no identifying contrast. Family-cluster sandwich SEs and the correlation delta method are conditional on thresholds and weights. parameter_order indexes free covariance entries and parameter_covariance their joint uncertainty. A boundary in any component withholds all normal SEs; the tolerance is max(1e-7, 10*sqrt(tol)). Correlations at or below that variance are NaN.

benchmarks/bench_pairwise_multi.py covers both correlation signs and nulls, A+C+M, MCAR, IPW and omitted shared environment. Its evidence is limited to the tested designs. Multi-trait scoring is A+E, so do not pass a C/M fit's rp as full_corrmat: that would incorrectly treat shared covariance as residual E.

docs.title: Ascertained samples
docs.text:
The HE dose-response (bench_ascertainment.py, nuclear families, true h² = 0.5, K = 0.05, N = 2,000, two replicates) shows why selection matters:

realised case share ÷ assumed K 0.95× 1.51× 1.96× ≥ 2× fitted h² 0.420 0.984 0.998 1.000

This is bias, not just noise: the proband-ascertained arm remains at +0.500 bias from N = 1,000 to 10,000 and across initial values. See RESULTS §29.

docs.title: When you can correct it: sampling="ipw"
docs.text:
For a known design with positive inclusion probability π in every stratum, pass weights = 1 / π:

import numpy as np
from ltpred import fit_heritability

# 50/50 case/control cohort from population prevalence K = 0.05:
keep_p = 0.05 * 0.5 / (0.5 * 0.95)
weights = np.where(proband_is_case, 1.0, 1.0 / keep_p)
fit = fit_heritability(families, sampling="ipw", weights=weights)

Augmentation within a given family is already conditional on its statuses; selection breaks the mix of families, which the weights restore. In the benchmark this returns case-enriched fits from the boundary to near the true 0.5.

Two limits remain:

  • Positivity. No finite weight reconstructs a stratum with zero inclusion probability. Ascertainment through an affected proband is the standard failure. Weighted marginal case rates provide a diagnostic warning; they cannot establish invalid weights or joint positivity.
  • Efficiency. At K = 0.05 a 50/50 cohort needs weights up to 19×, greatly reducing effective sample size. IPW buys accuracy with precision.

ltpred cannot infer weights from the data. Family-history selection is correctable only when every complete observed family pattern has a known, strictly positive inclusion probability.

A scale correction is not a selection model

A Lee observed→liability factor depends only on (K, P) and cannot repair these fits: at fixed K, true h² = 0 and 0.5 can both return 1.000, so no invertible constant maps both back. The fitters already estimate on the liability scale. Use observed_to_liability_h2 only to convert an observed-scale estimate from another method.

docs.title: Sensitivity to the assumed heritability
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from ltpred import estimate_liability
grid = [0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7]
scores = [estimate_liability(families, h2=h).est["genetic"] for h in grid]
min_corr = np.corrcoef(scores)[np.triu_indices(len(grid), 1)].min()

In the calibration benchmark, assumed h² 0.2–0.8 barely changed ranking (corr with true g 0.429–0.431) while the calibration slope moved from 2.24 to 0.68: it acted mostly as a near-linear rescaling in that design, not as proof of rank invariance. Probe prevalence/CIP sensitivity by rebuilding the bounds and comparing scores. Low cross-setting correlation is a reason to seek a better external estimate or, only under the sampling contract, fit one.

docs.title: Variance components (A / C / M)
docs.text:
from ltpred import fit_variance_components
vc = fit_variance_components(families, ("A", "C"), sampling="population")
vc.components["A"], vc.components["C"], vc.residual

C is identified only by full-sib pairs. vc.se has the same Monte-Carlo-only meaning as h2_se; use bootstrap_fit for sampling uncertainty. With ("A",) the result matches fit_heritability.

M loads on genetically unrelated mate pairs (parents and grandparent couples). It describes spousal resemblance from shared adult environment and/or assortative mating but is not a generative assortative-mating model. Because mates have A = 0, omitting M usually biases A much less than omitting C. Every identifying pair set must be present. Dominance is unsupported because the role bank provides no independent dominance kernel. C and M kernels are PSD equivalence-class partitions with unit diagonal; residual variance is 1 - sum(components), floored at eps.
